title: Efficacy and safety of single-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for the curative treatment of extracranial primary Tumors: A collaborative systematic review on behalf of the SBRT Focus Group of the European Society for Radiotherapy & Oncology (ESTRO).
authors: Cuccia F, Franzese C, Dubash S, Dionisi V, Brunner T, Cellini F, Hörner-Rieber J, Zilli T
abstract: Single-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SF-SBRT) represents one of the most advanced frontiers in modern radiation oncology. While ultra-hypofractionation has entered everyday clinical practice in different fields of the oncological care, curative treatments in one session are increasingly attractive for the potential favorable combination of logistic advantages with safety and clinical outcomes. This collaborative systematic review promoted by the ESTRO SBRT Focus Group in participation with members of different disease-site Focus Groups collects the available data in support of SF-SBRT for the curative treatment of the main extracranial primary tumors. The findings highlight that, for specific anatomical sites, SF-SBRT is both safe and effective though the results emphasize the critical importance of careful patient selection and mandatory technological requirements for treatment planning and delivery. This collaborative work provides a comprehensive overview of current evidence and identifies key knowledge gaps for future investigation and upcoming clinical trials.

title: The impact of prophylactic azithromycin on the developing preterm gut microbiome and resistome.
authors: Ahearn-Ford S, Aboklaish A, Young GR, Lowe J, Masi AC, Gallacher D, Marchesi JR, Berrington JE
abstract: Early-life antibiotic exposure can profoundly impact the developing preterm gut microbiome and resistome, with short- and long-term consequences for health. In a large multi-center (n = 28) study of 693 preterm infants, we investigated the effects of 10 d of prophylactic intravenous azithromycin on the gut microbiome and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). The AZithromycin ThErapy for Chronic Lung Disease of Prematurity (AZTEC) study was a double blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of preterm infants (born < 30 weeks of gestation), treated from birth for 10 d with either intravenous azithromycin or placebo, and sampled longitudinally for 21 d or discharge. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, antibiotic susceptibility testing, and quantitative PCR, we show azithromycin reduced microbial diversity and the relative abundance of health-associated Bifidobacterium and increased relative abundances of pathobionts Staphylococcus and Enterobacter/Klebsiella. This early azithromycin treatment increased the number of macrolide-resistant genes, including the presence of erm (C), which persisted for the duration of the study. Probiotic use (at individual unit discretion) increased alpha diversity and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, but did not fully mitigate the effects of azithromycin receipt. Combined azithromycin and probiotics further increased the enrichment of Enterobacter/Klebsiella and total ARGs, including erm(C). These findings highlight the impacts of antibiotic and probiotic use, both important in balancing infection control issues and microbiome disruption and antimicrobial resistance.

title: Effects on health and antioxidant status of oral supplementation of hazelnut skin extract in dairy calves with neonatal diarrhea: a randomized clinical trial in hospitalized patients.
authors: Boccardo A, Sannazzaro M, Sala G, Gazzola E, Martucci I, Curone G, Castrica M, Ferrulli V
abstract: Neonatal calf diarrhea (NCD) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in calves. Growing concern about antimicrobial resistance has spurred interest in phytotherapeutic alternatives, particularly polyphenol-rich extracts. Hazelnut skin (HS), a by-product of the confectionery sector, is a sustainable and underutilized source of polyphenols; however, its therapeutic efficacy in calves with NCD remains insufficiently investigated. This randomized, parallel-group clinical trial evaluated the effects of oral HS extract supplementation as an adjunct to standard medical therapy in hospitalized dairy calves with NCD. Sixty female Holstein calves were randomly allocated to a control group (CTRL; n = 30) or a treatment group (HS; n = 30) receiving 10 g/day of HS extract with milk for 5 days. All calves received standardized clinical management, including fluid therapy and antimicrobial administration. Clinical parameters, milk intake, body weight, hospitalization outcomes, sepsis scores, and blood oxidative stress biomarkers were monitored. No significant differences were detected between groups for clinical recovery, fecal score, hydration status, milk intake, weight gain, hospitalization duration, mortality, or oxidative stress markers. Clinical improvement over time was evident in both groups and was attributable to standard therapy. In conclusion, short-term oral supplementation with HS extract did not confer additional clinical or antioxidant benefits when added to conventional treatment in calves with NCD.

title: Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic syndrome and suicidal death in a nationwide cohort study.
authors: Huh H, Kang MW, Lee J, Oh J, Kim M, Koh JH, Kwon JK, Cho JM
abstract: BACKGROUND: Individual cardiometabolic diseases are associated with psychiatric conditions and suicide. However, the association between the recently proposed Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome framework and suicide-related mortality remains unevaluated. METHODS: We analyzed data from 4,601,001 participants in the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, categorizing CKM health into Stages 0-4. The association between CKM stages and suicide-related mortality was evaluated using multivariable Cox regression with sequential adjustment for clinicodemographic variables, comorbidity, and claims-based psychiatric diagnoses, and using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models treating non-suicide death as a competing event. RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 10.11 years, 12,034 suicidal death events occurred. After adjustment, advanced CKM stages were associated with an increased risk of suicidal death (stage 3: adjusted HR 1.328, 95% CI 1.217-1.449; stage 4: adjusted HR 1.319, 95% CI 1.220-1.426), and the association persisted after further adjustment for other psychiatric disorders. Estimates were attenuated but remained significant in Fine-Gray models accounting for the competing risk of non-suicide death (stage 3: subdistribution HR 1.199, 95% CI 1.098-1.310; stage 4: 1.246, 95% CI 1.150-1.349). Exploratory subgroup analyses indicated that the association was most pronounced in younger adults aged 20-39 and in individuals without a claims-based diagnosis of depression. CONCLUSIONS: Advanced CKM syndrome is associated with increased suicide-related mortality. Mental health surveillance within the clinical management of CKM dysfunction may serve as a potential preventive strategy. Future studies are needed to evaluate the utility of CKM-based risk stratification in suicidal death prevention.

title: Comorbid asthma - occurrence and associations with patient-related outcomes in COPD: a cohort study.
authors: Athlin Å, Lisspers K, Hasselgren M, Ställberg B, Sandelowsky H, Giezeman M, Janson C, Kisiel MA
journal: Scandinavian journal of primary health care
abstract: PURPOSE: Clinical features of COPD and asthma overlap, complicating differential diagnosis. This study investigated the prevalence of comorbid asthma in COPD patients and its association with patient-related outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients with a doctor's diagnosis of COPD were randomly selected in two cohorts 2005 (n = 1060) and 2014 (n = 1671), from primary and secondary care in Sweden. Data were collected from medical records and patient questionnaires at baseline and at follow-up (2012 and 2022, respectively). Questionnaires included data on exacerbations. Symptoms were assessed using the clinical COPD questionnaire (CCQ). Comorbid asthma was identified through medical records. Ten-year mortality data were obtained from national registers. Logistic and linear regression assessed associations with patient-reported outcomes; Cox regression was applied for mortality analyses. RESULTS: Comorbid asthma was found in 22% of the 2005 cohort and 9% of the 2014 cohort (p < .001). In both cohorts, it was associated with an increased risk of exacerbations: OR (95% CI) 1.58 (1.07-2.32), p = .02, and 2.20 (1.38-3.52), p < .001, respectively. No associations were found between comorbid asthma and worsening of health status (CCQ). Mortality risk did not differ in the 2005 cohort, HR (95% CI) 0.92 (0.71-1.18), but was lower in the 2014 cohort, HR (95% CI) 0.67 (0.49-0.93), p = .02. CONCLUSION: Comorbid asthma in COPD has changed from 22 to 9%, potentially due to improved diagnostics. Comorbid asthma remains clinically relevant due to its association with an increased exacerbation risk.

title: Dose-related cardiac side effects and its impact on survival following thoracic radiotherapy: A scoping review.
authors: Fidan U, Hessels AC, Crijns APG, Wijsman R, van der Meer P, Langendijk JA, Muijs CT, van Luijk P
abstract: Radiation dose to the heart is associated with various cardiac side effects. However, the specific cardiac and pulmonary structures that contribute to these toxicities remain incompletely understood. Moreover, although multiple factors contribute to reduced survival after radiotherapy, the role of radiation-induced cardiac toxicity remains underrecognized. This scoping review aimed to evaluate the associations between radiation dose to specific cardiac and pulmonary structures, cardiac side effects, and survival. A total of 137 clinical studies were analysed in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Associations between radiation dose and cardiac side effects were identified not only for the whole heart but also for specific cardiac substructures, including myocardial segments, coronary arteries, and the pericardium. Notably, radiation dose to the lungs was also associated with decline in cardiac function, suggesting that minimizing cardiac toxicity may require consideration of both local cardiac irradiation and non-local irradiation of adjacent organs, particularly the lungs. Direct evidence linking cardiac side effects to survival was limited. Nevertheless, the observed associations between higher radiation doses, increased cardiac toxicity, and poorer survival suggest a potential relationship that warrants further investigation. These findings support the hypothesis that reducing specific cardiac side effects may benefit from targeted sparing of the relevant cardiac and pulmonary substructures. While many radiation-related cardiac side effects are now recognized, further research is needed to identify and characterize previously unrecognized manifestations and to clarify their contribution to long-term survival.

title: Gut microbiota shaping fatty liver disease progression.
authors: Wysokińska M, Mysza M, Uryga AE, Kołodziejczyk AA
abstract: The gut-liver axis is an important regulator of homeostasis, and its dysregulation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). In this review, we summarize current knowledge on both compositional alterations of the gut microbiome in MASLD and the functional consequences of these changes. We first discuss changes across major microbial domains, including bacteria, archaea, eukaryota, and bacteriophages, and then focus on microbiota-derived metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, trimethylamine and its derivative trimethylamine N-oxide, tryptophan-derived indoles, secondary bile acids, and other bioactive compounds. Their complex impacts on intestinal barrier integrity, inflammation, lipid and glucose metabolism, and immune and hormonal signaling in the liver are highlighted. We further examine mechanisms involving the translocation of microbial products and the modulation of nuclear and membrane receptors. Finally, we outline current challenges and knowledge gaps that need to be addressed to better understand the role of the gut microbiota in MASLD.

title: Functionally declining microbiota in chronic disease: beyond taxonomic loss.
authors: Kim HS
abstract: Microbiota deterioration in modern human populations has been linked to chronic disease, and taxonomic profiling is increasingly used to understand, diagnose, and guide treatment. Yet such profiles do not fully capture disease-relevant microbiota states. I propose functional decline within retained taxa as a distinct axis of microbiota deterioration, complementary to taxonomic loss. Modern environmental pressures can drive not only taxonomic loss but also directional selection toward variants or lineages with reduced host-beneficial function or increased harmful activity. Two mechanistically characterized systems from studies by my group illustrate this process: antibiotic-selected Akkermansia variants with diminished metabolic benefits, and Faecalibacterium pathobionts that promote disease when dominant over beneficial strains, with supporting evidence from atopic dermatitis and pediatric inflammatory bowel disease. Evidence from additional gut taxa suggests that this pattern may extend beyond these two examples. By integrating this hidden axis of functional decline with the well-established axis of taxonomic loss, the proposed two-axis framework could help clarify inconsistent microbiota-disease associations and guide strain-resolved, function-first approaches to microbiota analysis and intervention.

title: DiFVM: A Vectorized Graph-Based Finite Volume Solver for Differentiable CFD on Unstructured Meshes.
authors: Du P, Li Y, Xu M, Wang JX
abstract: Differentiable programming has emerged as an important tool for gradient-based inverse problems and end-to-end hybrid physics-machine learning in computational fluid dynamics. Existing differentiable CFD platforms predominantly rely on structured Cartesian grids, limiting their direct application to geometrically complex domains where body-conforming unstructured discretizations are essential. We present DiFVM, the first GPU-native, end-to-end differentiable finite-volume (FV) CFD solver for incompressible flow on unstructured polyhedral meshes. The central methodological contribution is a graph-based computational reformulation of the complete unstructured FV/PISO solution procedure: by expressing FV operators as static scatter/gather primitives on the mesh connectivity graph, DiFVM transforms irregular unstructured connectivity into a GPU-compatible computational representation. All operations are implemented in JAX/XLA, providing just-in-time compilation, operator fusion, and automatic differentiation through the complete simulation pipeline. Differentiable Windkessel outlet boundary conditions are provided for cardiovascular applications, and DiFVM accepts standard OpenFOAM case directories without modification for seamless adoption in existing workflows. Forward accuracy is assessed through analytical and canonical benchmark problems, comparisons with published reference data, and independent solver comparisons, while end-to-end differentiability is demonstrated through proof-of-concept inverse modeling examples. DiFVM provides a differentiable CFD framework for gradient-based optimization, inverse modeling and future physics-integrated machine learning on complex unstructured geometries.

title: Sensitive detection of 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal-modified proteins in oxidative stress-related diseases.
authors: Méndez-Cuadro D, Kamali AN, Ruiz C, Pérez-Benavente S, Hernáez ML, Rodríguez-Cavallo E, Puyet A, Bautista JM
abstract: Protein modification by 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (HNE) is associated with metabolic, neurodegenerative, and infectious diseases characterized by oxidative stress. Detecting low-abundance HNE-protein adducts in complex extracts requires antibodies with suitable reactivity and selectivity. We generated polyclonal antisera in rabbits using matched-species rabbit serum albumin modified in vitro with HNE (RSA-HNE), administered either intact or after tryptic digestion. The antisera displayed distinct recognition profiles across dot blot, ELISA, and Western blot assays using HNE-modified standards and membrane-protein extracts from uninfected and Plasmodium falciparum-infected human erythrocytes. Antiserum 1, raised against intact RSA-HNE, showed the stronger overall immunochemical response, whereas Antiserum 2, raised against tryptic RSA-HNE, displayed a different and more restricted peptide-recognition profile. In an immunoenrichment and LC-MS/MS workflow, Antiserum 1 recovered 14 candidate HNE-associated membrane proteins from erythrocytes infected with P. falciparum trophozoites. Site-specific evidence remained tentative for four peptides. These antisera are therefore proposed as research tools for studying protein lipoxidation, although biological replication and orthogonal validation of the candidate modification sites are required.

title: CATH-1 supplementation improves sperm quality and fertility of rooster semen during cold storage by reducing bacterial contamination.
authors: Authaida S, Boonkum W, Duangjinda M, Shimada M, Kaeoket K, Rerkyusuke S, Chankitisakul V
abstract: The present study investigated the effects of antibiotic and antimicrobial peptide supplementation on semen quality, viable bacterial load, and fertility potential in Thai native chickens during cold storage. Semen samples were diluted in an extender supplemented with kanamycin (31.20 μg/mL) or CATH-1 (3.75 or 7.50 μg/mL) and stored at 5 °C for up to 72 h. Sperm quality parameters, viable bacterial load, and reproductive outcomes following artificial insemination were assessed at 0, 24, 48, and 72 h. Storage duration significantly affected all sperm quality parameters (P < 0.001), while fertility and hatchability were progressively lower across the sequential storage-time phases. Kanamycin and CATH-1 at 3.75 μg/mL consistently maintained higher sperm quality and reduced susceptibility to lipid peroxidation compared with the control (P < 0.05), with no significant difference between the two treatments. Both treatments effectively suppressed bacterial proliferation; however, viable bacterial load increased progressively beyond 24 h in all groups. Scanning electron microscopy revealed marked bacterial surface alterations following CATH-1 treatment, consistent with membrane-disruptive antibacterial activity. In contrast, CATH-1 at 7.50 μg/mL compromised sperm quality and reproductive outcomes from the initial time point onward, despite achieving the greatest bacterial suppression among all treatments. Across the sequential storage-time phases, fertility potential was progressively lower, although the kanamycin and CATH-1 (3.75 μg/mL) groups maintained higher fertility than the control during prolonged storage. These findings demonstrate a dose-dependent dual effect of CATH-1, with 3.75 μg/mL performing comparably to kanamycin and representing a promising antibiotic alternative in the context of One Health concerns in poultry artificial insemination programs.

title: Balancing individual risks and collective benefits: Effects of vaccine price, message framing, and value orientations on influenza vaccination in China.
authors: Chu Y, Jiang Y, Cheng Q, Zha X, Wang Y, Liang W, Chen L
abstract: Vaccines are widely recognized as effective tools for preventing infectious diseases; however, vaccine hesitancy remains a persistent global challenge that undermines herd immunity and public health efforts. This study investigates how message framing and value orientation impact Chinese university students' willingness to receive the influenza vaccination at different price points, aiming to inform strategies for promoting health behaviors. A 2 (framing: gain, loss) ×2 (value orientation: individualism, collectivism) experimental design was employed with 1,408 Chinese university students to examine influences on vaccination intention. Vaccination intention decreased significantly as vaccine price increased. Compared with the control group, persuasive messages generally increased vaccination intention, and this effect became more pronounced in paid scenarios. When the vaccine was free, differences among message types were not significant. In paid scenarios, loss-framed messages were more persuasive than gain-framed messages, and individualistic-oriented messages were more effective than collectivistic-oriented messages. Among the four message combinations, the individualistic-loss message showed the strongest persuasive effect. Mediation analyses further indicated that perceived severity of influenza and perceived vaccine effectiveness mediated the effect of the individualistic-loss message on vaccination intention. Vaccination intention is influenced by the interaction between vaccine price and message attributes. Free vaccination reduces the relative impact of message variations, whereas paid scenarios provide more room for persuasive messages to operate. In price-sensitive contexts, individualistic-loss messages that emphasize personal infection risks and vaccine effectiveness may be particularly useful for promoting influenza vaccination.

title: "If I've got this, then let me use it to try to help and change it." Perspectives on HIV cure and research participation: a qualitative interview study of women and migrants living with HIV in Australia.
authors: Mihiri W, Susan Cs C, Kirsten M, Heather E, Ian John W, Jennifer P, Jillian Sy L
abstract: BACKGROUND: People living with HIV who are women and/or migrants are underrepresented in cure-related trials, raising equity, acceptability, and research generalisability concerns (including those related to HIV clade representation). OBJECTIVE: Explore perspectives of HIV cure-related research amongs a cohort of women and migrants people living with HIV. METHODS: Alongside HIV community groups, people living with HIV who identified as women and/or spoke a non-English language at home attending infectious diseases clinic at a tertiary academic hospital in Melbourne, Australia were interviewed. These explored cure research knowledge and perceptions, participation motivations/barriers, and trial design preferences. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed thematically using an inductive approach. RESULTS: Twenty interviews were completed (four with interpreters). Median age was 50.5 years (range 32-75). Fourteen participants identified as female and six as male; 15 were born outside Australia. HIV cure research awareness was limited. Most described ongoing physical, psychological, and social impacts from HIV, reinforcing desire for a cure. Established relationships with HIV clinicians were central to research engagement. Additional motivators included personal benefit and altruism. Conversely, perceived risks, time commitments, and fear of unwanted sharing of HIV status were barriers. Participants emphasised culturally appropriate communication and meaningful community involvement is needed. CONCLUSION: These participants view cure research with hope and hesitation. Equitable participation requires addressing structural and cultural barriers, improving communication, and embedding community perspectives into research. HIV providers are vital partners, working alongside communities to support informed decision-making, and help ensure that the path toward an HIV cure is shaped by, and for, those it serves.

Circulatory arrest versus aortic cross-clamping in proximal thoracic aortic aneurysm repair.
authors: Braatz E, Stenman M, Al-Mousli J, Dalén M, Olsson C
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Aortic cross‑clamping and mild hypothermic circulatory arrest (MHCA) are commonly used strategies in proximal thoracic aortic aneurysm surgery. This study compared these approaches in elective procedures for patients with a distal ascending aortic diameter of 40-50 mm. The primary outcome was a composite of 30‑day mortality, stroke, or acute kidney injury, with secondary outcomes including long‑term survival and postoperative complications. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This single‑center observational cohort included patients treated between 2016 and 2024. Distal ascending aortic diameters were assessed on preoperative computed tomography, and clinical data were obtained from SWEDEHEART. Patients were assigned to aortic cross‑clamp (n = 261) or MHCA (n = 138). Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 ratio to balance baseline characteristics. RESULTS: The composite primary outcome occurred in 15 patients (3.8%) and was more common with MHCA than with cross‑clamp (6.5% vs 2.3%, p = 0.035). Two patients (0.5%), both in the MHCA group, died within 30 days. After matching, the odds ratio for the composite endpoint was 2.4 (95% CI, 0.66-11.5), indicating no significant difference. Long‑term survival was similar between groups (log‑rank p = 0.33). CONCLUSIONS: Both strategies were associated with low perioperative risk and comparable long‑term survival. These results support flexible operative planning, allowing the distal anastomotic technique to be chosen based on individual anatomy and surgical preference.

title: YBX3 promotes ischemia-reperfusion injury by enhancing microglial glycolysis via PKM2 stabilization and mTOR-HIF-1α pathway activation.
authors: Feng Z, Qin P, Ni H, Cao X, Xu J, Yuan Y
abstract: Stroke remains one of the leading causes of death and long-term disability worldwide, with neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction playing central roles in its pathogenesis. In this study, we investigated the function of Y-box binding protein 3 (YBX3) in ischemic stroke, with particular focus on its regulation of glycolysis and neuroinflammatory responses. Using a middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model in C57BL/6 mice and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) model in BV2 microglia, we observed that YBX3 expression was markedly upregulated following ischemia-reperfusion. Overexpression of YBX3 aggravated cerebral infarct size, worsened motor and neurological outcomes, and increased the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β) both in vivo and in vitro. Mechanistically, YBX3 enhanced glycolysis in BV2 cells by stabilizing pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) mRNA and promoting its expression, while simultaneously activating glycolysis through the mTOR-HIF-1α signaling pathway. Pharmacological inhibition of mTOR with rapamycin reversed YBX3-induced glycolytic activation, neuroinflammation, and neuronal injury. Collectively, these results identify YBX3 as a key regulator of ischemic brain damage through glycolysis-dependent mechanisms and underscore its potential as a therapeutic target for stroke.

title: Depressive symptom profiles and risk of cardiometabolic disease incidence.
authors: Zwiep JC, Milaneschi Y, Vinkers CH, Giltay EJ, Schroevers RA, Penninx BWJH, Lamers F
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Major depressive disorder (MDD) has been linked to increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease (CMD). Depressive symptom profiles associated with inflammation (atypical energy-related symptoms (AES), anhedonia) may carry specific cardiometabolic risk. We investigated whether MDD, AES and anhedonia are associated with higher CMD incidence compared to typical depressive symptoms and control participants. METHODS: Data were from the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety (NESDA), including participants with lifetime MDD and non-depressed controls, without baseline CMD (N = 1858). CMD incidence was established over 15-year follow-up using self-report, medication use, and glucose. AES, anhedonia, typical symptoms, and depression severity were derived from the Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology Self-Report. Cox proportional hazard models were adjusted for sociodemographic and lifestyle factors. RESULTS: CMD incidence rate was 21.3/1000 person years. MDD was associated with increased CMD incidence compared to controls (HR = 1.65, 95%CI: 1.30-2.11). In continuous analyses, only AES and depression severity were significantly associated with CMD incidence, though effect sizes were comparable across symptom profiles. When divided into severity tertiles and compared to controls, associations were largely similar across profiles, with no clear dose-response pattern. All profiles were associated with cardiovascular disease incidence, but only AES was associated with diabetes incidence. DISCUSSION: MDD is associated with CMD incidence over 15 years. Depressive symptom profiles did not show differential associations with CMD incidence. Effect sizes across profiles were comparable, suggesting a general rather than symptom-specific depression burden on cardiometabolic health risk. Continued monitoring of cardiometabolic risk factors is warranted for people with a history of depression.

title: Systems metabolic engineering of a plasmid-free Escherichia coli cell factory for high-level cytidine production.
authors: Zhao R, Li C, Xu C, Chen Z, Xiong H, Yu Z, Shi T, Li L
abstract: Cytidine is an important precursor for nucleoside pharmaceuticals, but its fermentative production is constrained by competing degradation, poor selectivity of pyrimidine flux, insufficient precursor supply, and energy-redox imbalance. In this study, a plasmid-free E. coli cell factory was constructed through systems metabolic engineering. Sequential deletion of cytidine degradation, salvage, and precursor-consuming pathways enabled initial cytidine accumulation. The conversion from UMP to CMP was strengthened by introducing feedback-deregulated pyrH D93A and pyrG D160E, E162A, E168K cgl mutants and nudG, while the heterologous expression of PHM8 sce improved CMP-to-cytidine conversion selectivity. Scaffold-based assembly of PyrF, PyrHD93A, NudG, and PHM8sce using CipA/CipB further improved local pathway channeling and reduced uridine formation by 98.70%. To reinforce upstream flux, de novo UMP biosynthesis was reconstructed with the B. subtilis pyr operon, PRPP synthesis was enhanced, and nitrogen-donor and pyrimidine-ring precursor supply was improved through glnA, ppc, and aspC expression. Finally, an ATP-responsive ydaO motif regulatory module was used to dynamically control respiratory-chain and oxygen-utilization modules, coordinating ATP supply with NAD+ regeneration. The final strain cyt 23 produced 96.20 g/L cytidine in 50 h in a 5 L fed-batch bioreactor, with a glucose conversion yield of 0.38 g/g and productivity of 1.92 g/(L·h), representing the highest reported titer, yield and productivity for microbial cytidine production to date. This work provides an integrated strategy for high-level microbial cytidine production and nucleoside cell-factory development.

title: Open-label extension study of leniolisib in activated PI3Kδ syndrome: Long-term efficacy and safety.
authors: Rao VK, Šedivá A, Dalm VASH, Plebani A, Schuetz C, Shcherbina A, Trizzino A, Zharankova Y
abstract: Activated phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta syndrome (APDS) is an inborn error of immunity characterized by immune deficiency and dysregulation. Leniolisib is a selective phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta inhibitor approved to treat APDS in patients ≥12 years old. We report final results from a single-arm, open-label extension study in 37 patients with APDS (NCT02859727). Median leniolisib exposure was 4.3 years (range, 1.2-7.0 years). Adverse events (AE) were reported in 34 patients; 87% were grade 1. Serious AEs, reported in 10 patients, were deemed unrelated to leniolisib. Two patients discontinued treatment due to AEs: cardiac arrest and Hodgkin's lymphoma. There were significant reductions in annual infection (P = 0.0005) and respiratory infection (P = 0.0017) rates per year of treatment. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IRT) use significantly decreased per year of treatment (P = 0.0095). Clinically meaningful improvements in general health scores from the 36-Item Short Form Survey were observed. Overall, long-term use of leniolisib was generally well tolerated, and infections and IRT use reduced over time.

title: Nutrient availability and sodium pyruvate regulate the resuscitation of viable but nonculturable Staphylococcus aureus.
authors: Yu H, Ge R, Du J, Hua Y, Zhao F
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) can enter a viable but nonculturable (VBNC) state when induced by citric acid at 4 °C, posing hidden risks to food safety upon resuscitation. However, the effects of nutritional conditions and sodium pyruvate (SP) on this process remain unclear. This study demonstrates that 0.5 × TSB, TSB, 2 × TSB, and SP resuscitate VBNC cells following sigmoidal kinetics, with an efficacy ranking of SP > 2 × TSB > TSB > 0.5 × TSB. SP significantly accelerated resuscitation through enhanced early enzymatic activity, a transient increase in intracellular ROS levels, and rapid ATP accumulation, accompanied by dynamic nucleic acid fluctuations peaking at 10-12 h. Furthermore, proteomic profiling and targeted inhibition analyses revealed that DNA repair and cell wall biosynthesis are critically involved in initiating resuscitation, whereas signal transduction and respiratory metabolism primarily govern post-resuscitation growth. Practically, a 5-h or 10-h pre-resuscitation in 2 × TSB successfully detected VBNC S. aureus in high pressure processing-treated apple juice during 4 °C storage, which was undetectable via direct enumeration. These findings offer mechanistic insights into pathogen resuscitation and provide practical strategies for food safety risk assessment and detection.

title: 45th International Symposium on Intensive Care & Emergency Medicine.
Gut microbiota and metabolic characteristics in PWHIV with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
authors: Liu H, Xu T, Guo Y, Zhou X, Yan C, Zhu B, Xie Y
abstract: The global prevalence of Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) among persons with HIV (PWHIV) is estimated at 34%. This study examined the influence of gut microbial and metabolic alterations in PWHIV with MASLD. We conducted 16S rRNA sequencing on 60 fecal samples (24 from HIV group and 36 from HIV-MASLD group) to assess microbial composition, and employed LC/MS-based metabolomics on both fecal and plasma samples to identify variations in metabolites. An exploratory analysis was performed to compare plasma cytokines and oxidative stress markers between the two groups. Sequencing in the HIV-MASLD group showed lower Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum, and higher Klebsiella, Escherichia, and Enterococcus. Metabolomic analysis revealed a reduction in anti-inflammatory metabolites (Dodecanedioic acid, 5-Phenylvaleric acid, Kynurenic acid) and antioxidant metabolites, coupled with an increase in the pro-inflammatory metabolite Gamma-Glutamyl-L-Putrescine in the HIV-MASLD group. And plasma analysis indicated a decline in 20-carboxy arachidonic acid. Additionally, Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum correlated positively with anti-inflammatory metabolites, while Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Citrobacter correlated negatively. Furthermore, Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum also showed a moderate negative correlation with MDA levels. A random forest model using plasma metabolites showed the optimal discriminative ability for HIV-MASLD (AUC = 0.819 ± 0.0059). Differences in gut microbiota and metabolites in PWHIV may affect MASLD progression by influencing inflammation and oxidative stress. Modulating gut microbiota, such as adding Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum, could be a treatment strategy for HIV-MASLD. Plasma metabolites have potential as noninvasive markers.

title: Targeted inhibition of inflammatory liver macrophages with a multifunctional nanoparticle ameliorates metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.
authors: Chen K, Wang L, Liu L, Arledge CA, Lin HK, Lin J, Habib AA, Zhao D
abstract: Despite metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) being a significant global health concern, there are few effective ways to prevent or treat MASH. Evidence from preclinical and clinical studies suggests that inflammatory polarization of Kupffer cells (KCs) and infiltration of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) in liver macrophages play an essential role in the initiation and progression of MASH. Herein, we reported a liposomal nanoparticle (NP-OMg) that targets suppressive oligodeoxynucleotide (sODN) and magnesium ions (Mg2+) to KCs and MDMs. sODN acted as a potent inhibitor of multiple pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), while Mg2+ was chosen for its anti-oxidative and anti-pyroptotic effects, and its capability of coordinating with sODN in NP-OMg. Intravenously administrated NP-OMg was primarily engulfed by both KCs and MDMs in mouse liver. Therapeutically, NP-OMg mitigated hepatic steatosis, inflammation and fibrosis, and restored liver functions in mouse models of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)/MASH. Mechanistically, RNA-sequencing analysis revealed that NP-OMg largely reversed the aberrant gene expression and signaling pathways involved in the pathogenesis of MASLD/MASH. Through comprehensive targeting of inflammatory pathways in liver macrophages, NP-OMg treatment significantly reduced production of inflammatory cytokines/chemokines and decreased the liver recruitment of Ly6chigh inflammatory MDMs. These findings demonstrate the potential of a new liver macrophage-targeted nanomedicine strategy for the treatment of MASH.

title: Hematopoietic cell transplantation using treosulfan-based conditioning for IL-10 receptor deficiency.
authors: Lakkaraja M, Schmitt EG, Sood AK, Chen K, Modi AJ, Verbsky JW, Torgerson T, Wahbeh G
abstract: IL-10 receptor deficiency is a life-threatening inborn error of immunity associated with early-onset inflammatory bowel disease. Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) using treosulfan-based conditioning resulted in excellent survival with full donor engraftment. Importantly, anakinra effectively served as a bridge to HCT.

title: Acute liver injury is triggered by dysbiosis and microbial translocation involving gut-liver axis.
authors: Halder U, Hamida H, Kakar K, Yang X, Zhong Y, Nagarkatti M, Nagarkatti P
abstract: Acute liver injury (ALI) is a severe clinical condition that can progress to chronic liver failure, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma, yet therapeutic options remain limited. Here, we investigated how hepatotoxin-induced gut-liver dysbiosis drives hepatic inflammation through microbial crosstalk. Using three murine ALI models, we assessed liver injury, intestinal barrier integrity, microbial composition along the gut-liver axis, and immune activation. Each hepatotoxin recapitulated distinct features of human ALI and induced unique patterns of hepatic and intestinal injury, enabling the progressive translocation of live bacteria from the gut to the liver and bloodstream. ALI was consistently associated with depletion of commensal taxa (Lactobacillaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Bifidobacteriaceae) and enrichment of opportunistic pathogens (Enterococcaceae, Clostridiaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, and Burkholderiaceae). Dysbiosis also involved reduced gut bacteriophages and the expansion of viral families, including Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, in the liver and blood. Transplantation of the fecal or liver microbiota from ALI mice into microbiota-depleted recipients reproduced liver injury, immune activation, and intestinal barrier disruption, demonstrating that dysbiotic microbial communities alone are sufficient to trigger hepatic inflammation. These communities activated Th1/Th17 associated pathways (NF-κB, IL-17, TGF-β, and antigen presentation networks) and expanded pro-inflammatory immune populations. A key advance of this study is the direct comparison of fecal- versus liver-derived microbiota, revealing distinct mechanistic roles for each in driving liver pathology. Across all models, hepatotoxin-induced intestinal barrier breakdown drives gut-liver dysbiosis, microbial translocation, and immune-mediated liver injury. These findings uncover a unifying mechanism by which microbial imbalance reprograms hepatic immunity and accelerates ALI progression.

title: Abstracts
Special Collection: Abstracts from IUNS-ICN Paris 2025
Integrated analysis identifies dysregulated secretory proteins and crotonylation profiles associated with immune regulation in IgA nephropathy.
authors: Chen J, Zhang W, Dai Y, Ma H, Ma J, Zou G, Yan Q, Hu G
abstract: BACKGROUND: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is the most prevalent primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, with 20%-40% of patients progressing to end-stage renal disease. However, the relationship between peripheral immune alterations and local renal injury, particularly with respect to the abundance patterns and post-translational modification signals of secretory proteins, remains incompletely characterized. METHODS: This study included 48 samples, consisting of renal tissue samples from 7 IgAN patients and 10 controls, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 6 patients with IgAN and 25 controls. Renal tissue and PBMC samples were analyzed by proteomic and crotonylation profiling, respectively. These datasets represent cohort-level feature integration rather than paired multi-omics correlation analyses performed within the same individuals. Immune secretory protein annotations from the Human Protein Atlas supported downstream interpretation. Differential abundance analysis, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, functional enrichment, transcription factor (TF) prediction, and compound enrichment analysis using the DSigDB and Enrichr platforms were performed to explore molecular features and database-derived compounds associated with IgAN. RESULTS: Compared with the corresponding control groups, 92 differentially abundant secreted proteins and 36 secretory proteins with differential protein-abundance-normalized Kcr signals were identified in IgAN patients. PPI network analysis prioritized FGA, FGB, A2M, APOA1, C3, HP, SERPINA1, APOB, FGG, and TF as exploratory hub candidates, while STAT1, PML, STAT5B, and MYH11 were computationally predicted as candidate upstream TFs. Compound enrichment analysis identified thapsigargin as a database-derived, hypothesis-generating compound related to the secretory protein network in IgAN. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides an integrative characterization of secretory protein abundance and crotonylation patterns in IgA nephropathy. The findings suggest candidate hub proteins and upstream TFs potentially associated with immune dysregulation in IgAN. Despite the limited sample size, these results offer exploratory molecular insights and provide a basis for future mechanistic and experimental studies. SIGNIFICANCE: Secretory proteins may contribute to immune dysregulation and renal injury in immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN), but their abundance patterns and lysine crotonylation (Kcr)-related features remain incompletely characterized. This study integrated renal tissue proteomics, peripheral blood mononuclear cell crotonylomics, public transcriptomics, and Human Protein Atlas annotations at the feature level across independent cohorts. Descriptive fold-change screening yielded 92 HPA-annotated secretory proteins in renal tissue and 36 secretory proteins containing 120 protein-abundance-normalized Kcr sites in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Network analysis prioritized ten exploratory hub candidates, while STAT1, PML, STAT5B, and MYH11 were computationally prioritized as candidate upstream transcription factors. DSigDB/Enrichr analysis further highlighted thapsigargin as a database-derived enrichment signal for hypothesis generation. These findings provide an exploratory molecular resource for investigating secretory protein abundance and Kcr-related patterns in IgAN. Because the datasets were unpaired and the proteomic and crotonylomic samples were pooled within groups, the results do not establish participant-level cross-tissue relationships, causal regulation, validated biomarkers, or therapeutic efficacy. Larger individual-level cohorts and functional studies are required for validation.

title: Hepatitis E virus in pig faeces, serum, excretory organs, and other edible tissues at slaughter in Spain, 2020-2022.
authors: García N, Santamaría-Palacios J, Hernández M, Cañete-Reyes A, Martínez I, Navarro A, Muñoz-Chimeno M, Elois MA
abstract: Foodborne hepatitis E is an emerging zoonosis in Europe, with domestic pigs recognized as the main reservoir of zoonotic hepatitis E virus (HEV) genotype 3. This study evaluated HEV circulation in Spain using a production-representative design (2020-2022). A total of 386 apparently healthy pigs from 11 large slaughterhouses (375 farms, 34 provinces) were analysed. Ten sample types (blood, faeces, liver, heart, kidney and 5 different muscles usually used to elaborate meat products) per animal (n = 3860) were tested for HEV RNA by RT-qPCR. Serum was also analysed for anti-HEV IgG by ELISA. Slaughterhouse wastewater was also screened to assess potential environmental dissemination. Overall seroprevalence reached 68.4%, indicating widespread HEV exposure among pigs. Of the 386 pigs analysed, 213 (55.2%) were positive for HEV RNA in at least one sample. HEV RNA was detected in 8.5% of all samples, most frequently in faeces (36.0%) and liver (16.3%), whereas lean meat and top loin were consistently negative, and only low positivity was found in rib meat samples (9.6%). Multivariable modelling using generalized estimating equations showed that HEV RNA detection was significantly more likely in faeces and liver (OR = 7.4 and 2.3, respectively) compared to kidney, while muscle and fat-rich cuts showed markedly lower odds. HEV RNA was also detected in six of seven wastewater samples, indicating potential environmental release through slaughterhouse effluents. Phylogenetic analysis of partial ORF2 sequences (n = 45) identified five HEV-3 subgenotypes: HEV-3f-A1, 3f-A2, 3c, 3f-B, 3e. These findings demonstrate active, genetically diverse HEV circulation in Spanish pigs, reinforcing the need for strengthened surveillance along the pork production chain.

title: Anp32e mediates histone variant H2A.Z-regulated TGF-β1 involvement in renal interstitial fibrosis.
authors: Zeng D, Tang C, Shan Y, Wei J, Liu Q, Yin X, Li Y
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
abstract: Renal interstitial fibrosis (RIF), a key pathological feature of chronic kidney disease, often leads to end-stage renal failure. However, the mechanisms underlying RIF remain unclear, and effective targeted therapies are still lacking. Our prior research identified that acidic nuclear phosphorylated protein 32 E (Anp32e) aggravates RIF, though the mechanism was not fully clarified. Anp32e is known as a histone chaperone regulating the histone variant H2A.Z, yet the role of H2A.Z in RIF and its connection to Anp32e remain largely unexplored. In this study, we observed elevated nuclear Anp32e in renal tubular epithelial cells in an RIF model. We further confirmed that Anp32e forms a protein complex with H2A.Z and showed that Anp32e may facilitates H2A.Z degradation via the proteasome pathway. Mechanistically, this degradation may reduce H2A.Z occupancy at the TGF-β1 promoter, leading to increased TGF-β1 expression and subsequent upregulation of fibrosis markers FN and Col-I. Collectively, our findings suggest that Anp32e may induces the degradation of H2A.Z via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which contribute to increased transcriptional activity of TGF-β1 and subsequent promotion of RIF.
